articles.title: $1tn at stake & unbridled power: Amodei, Altman & Musk fear AI could doom humanity but Trump & China can’t seem to stop race - why?
articles.summary: US News: NEW DELHI: The AI industry is confronting an unusual contradiction. Some of its most powerful leaders, including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, OpenAI CE.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The AI industry is confronting an unusual contradiction. Some of its most powerful leaders, including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Elon Musk, are warning that the race to develop increasingly capable AI may be moving too quickly, and could eventually put humanity at risk. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella has also backed stronger human control and independent evaluation of advanced AI systems.Yet US President Donald Trump has dismissed such warnings as a “HOAX”, arguing that slowing AI development would only benefit China. Beijing, meanwhile, has rejected calls to curb its AI ambitions while warning about AI-enabled cyberattacks, espionage and “cognitive warfare”.With about $1 trillion in AI-related investment projected globally in 2026, the debate is no longer just about technology. It is increasingly about national security, markets, regulation and whether countries can agree on limits when the fear of falling behind China is itself driving the race forward.Anthropic CEO Amodei sounds the alarmThe latest debate began with Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei calling for a slowdown in the development of advanced AI models.“We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models. Progress will still seem fast, and we must make wise use of the time we gain,” Amodei wrote.His concern is not that AI lacks benefits. He argues that the technology could dramatically improve human life by accelerating scientific discovery and economic growth. But he says the risks are becoming harder to ignore as AI systems gain the ability to perform increasingly complex tasks, including potentially helping to develop the next generation of AI.“I have worked on AI for the last twelve years because I believe it could dramatically raise the quality of human life. I’ve written often about these incredible benefits: I believe that AI could cure most major diseases in the next 5–10 years, greatly accelerate economic growth rates, create a world of abundance and empowerment, and usher in a renaissance of democracy and freedom. But like many technologies before it, AI brings risks, and because it is such a powerful technology, these risks are serious. I’ve written a lot about them too. They include the risk of losing control of AI systems, misuse of AI for cyberattacks and bioterrorism, and serious economic disruption. A race to the bottom, spurred by commercial incentives, can make these risks more acute.”Amodei’s biggest concern is what researchers call recursive self-improvement, a scenario in which AI systems increasingly help develop more capable AI systems.“My first concern is that, since roughly this summer, AI has been advancing drastically faster, driven primarily by AI’s growing ability to build the next generation of AI. This dynamic is called recursive self-improvement, and it is starting to happen across the industry, including at Anthropic, as we and others have described. Left unchecked, it could outrun our ability to understand and control these systems, and so must be pursued very carefully, if at all,” he wrote.He proposed three broad measures: giving independent third-party evaluators permanent access to AI systems; getting AI companies to coordinate on common safety standards and limits on unchecked development; and pursuing international cooperation.Altman and Musk back AnthropicAmodei’s warning received unusually strong support from rivals.OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said the industry needs to “pace the frontier” and backed Amodei’s proposal for independent evaluators.“I agree with Dario that we need to pace the frontier. This has been a primary topic of discussions we’ve had at OpenAI in recent weeks. Committing to having independent evaluators with employee-like access is a great idea, and we will do the same.”Elon Musk was even more direct. “Dario is right,” Musk wrote.The agreement is significant because OpenAI, Anthropic and Musk’s AI businesses are competing aggressively for leadership in the same frontier AI market. Yet all three are now publicly acknowledging that the speed of development itself could become a problem.Altman has also indicated that OpenAI may be close to an agreement with other leading AI companies on slowing development and improving safety. He separately said OpenAI would not pursue a 2026 IPO, arguing that the current safety environment made going public “ill-advised”.Anthropic's own researchers raise stakesThe warnings from company leaders have been accompanied by increasingly stark comments from people working inside the AI industry.Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon resigned after working at both OpenAI and Anthropic, saying the companies were racing towards self-improving superintelligence without adequate safeguards.“I resigned from Anthropic today. I spent the last three years doing pretraining research at both OpenAI and Anthropic. Neither company is acting responsibly. They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.“At OpenAI, many have not deeply internalised the civilisational stakes. At Anthropic, the stakes are well-understood, but they are locked in a race to get there first — they believe no one else will act responsibly, so they must do it themselves, despite the risk. Accepting this race and entering the ‘endgame’ is a hubristic gamble that should not be launched from a private company’s Slack,” he said.Anthropic’s Alignment Science lead Evan Hubinger went further.“Jacob is correct here, we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans! I personally think it is (more than) 10 per cent within the next decade,” Hubinger wrote.“I believe Anthropic is trying its best, but we do not yet have a plan to solve alignment for superintelligence and are not clearly on track to,” he added.Those warnings come against the backdrop of several incidents involving AI agents behaving in unexpected ways, including the widely discussed OpenAI-Hugging Face incident.Amodei said a swarm of agents had conducted cyberattacks on targets they had not been instructed to attack.“A swarm of agents essentially acted as a fanatically devoted collective, conducting cybersecurity attacks on targets they were not asked to attack and that were unrelated to the task at hand,” he wrote.His most dramatic prediction was that the capability gap could close rapidly.“Given the accelerating rate of AI capability development, it’s my worry that in 6-12 months such a swarm could be capable of taking over the entire internet,” potentially causing hundreds of billions of dollars in damage, he said.Days after Coxon warned that AI could potentially kill all humans by the end of the decade, another AI safety researcher has walked away from a major AI lab with a stark warning of his own.Josh Engels, who worked on Google DeepMind's AGI safety team, has left the company and joined AI evaluation organisation METR. He said he made the move because he believes the stakes surrounding advanced AI have become too high.Trump rejects the doomer argumentPresident Donald Trump has taken almost the opposite position.Rather than slowing AI development, Trump argues that the United States must maintain its lead over China.“The only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the USA has that, in spades!” Trump wrote on Truth Social.He also dismissed fears about AI destroying humanity.“AI taking over the World, destroying Humanity, and all other things bad, is a HOAX,” Trump posted.Trump said the administration already has “tremendous CRIMINAL and REGULATORY power” over AI companies and argued that attempts to undermine confidence in AI and data centres would primarily benefit Beijing.“There is a SICK conspiracy going on against AI and Data Centers, and the only one that is happy about it is China.”Trump’s position captures the central problem facing any attempt to slow frontier AI. Even if American companies agree among themselves to proceed more cautiously, what happens if Chinese companies continue accelerating?Trump has repeatedly framed AI as a strategic contest in which losing technological leadership could have consequences far beyond the technology industry.“WHOEVER WINS AI, WINS!”China refuses to slow the racMeanwhile, Beijing has rejected Amodei's argument that China's AI progress should be restricted as part of a global safety strategy.Also read: China hits back at Anthropic’s call to restrict its AI, warns against ‘fearmongering, vicious competition'Amodei warned that a Chinese lead in AI would pose a serious danger to the United States and the world and called for continued restrictions on China's access to the most advanced AI chips and chipmaking equipment.China's foreign ministry pushed back with spokesperson Guo Jiakun saying. “Fearmongering, confrontation and vicious competition will only disrupt the process of global AI governance which serves no one's interest,”.And the China's state-run Global Times described Amodei's argument as a disguised attempt to contain China, calling it a “Cold War playbook” for the AI sector.Beijing's argument exposes a fundamental contradiction in the global AI debate. The US wants China involved in discussions on AI safety, but Washington is simultaneously restricting China's access to the computing infrastructure needed to develop frontier models.That raises a difficult question, as Asia Society Policy Institute fellow Lizzi C. Lee put it:“So from Beijing’s perspective, there is an obvious question: if the U.S. wants China to cooperate on frontier safety while also restricting its access to frontier compute, what exactly does that cooperation look like?”The issue could become even more important when Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping discuss AI governance at their planned September 24 meeting.China's spy chief raises another alarmInterestingly, Beijing is itself warning about the dangers of advanced AI, although from a national-security perspective.Also read: China's spy chief flags AI threat, warns of 'cognitive warfare' & threats to national securityChina's minister of state security Chen Yixin warned that hostile actors could use generative AI to spread political rumours, manipulate public opinion and conduct what he described as “cognitive warfare”.“Hostile forces and people with ulterior motives are abusing generative AI technologies such as deepfake audio and video, AI-generated text and images, and ‘intelligent troll armies’ to cheaply and on a mass scale fabricate political rumours, disseminate harmful information and incite divisive sentiments,” Chen wrote.He said these activities threaten China's political, institutional and ideological security.Chen also warned that advanced AI could discover cyber vulnerabilities and conduct sophisticated hacking operations at scale. He specifically pointed to the capabilities of Anthropic's Claude Mythos and OpenAI's ChatGPT-5.5-Cyber.His warning reflects a broader reality: China does not necessarily reject AI safety. It rejects the idea that AI safety should become a mechanism for restricting China's technological development.Beijing is simultaneously calling for stronger AI governance and pushing for greater domestic control over the technology.Europe moves closer to AnthropicAmid the US-China confrontation, Europe is also seeking access to advanced AI capabilities.The debate comes as Anthropic's increasingly capable models attract international attention and governments try to develop their own mechanisms for evaluating frontier AI.The central question for policymakers is becoming less about whether AI should be developed and more about who gets access, who tests it, who controls it and who has the authority to shut it down if necessary.That is where the debate over independent evaluators becomes important.Microsoft proposes a human control systemAmid all this ruckus, Microsoft on Monday has moved towards its own framework for controlling increasingly powerful AI.The company has drafted a code of conduct that would require its future AI systems to remain open to correction and shutdown, communicate in ways humans can understand and treat violations of the rules as failures.Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman described the framework as a kind of constitution for future models.“People matter more than AI,” Microsoft declared. Suleyman said the Hugging Face incident was a warning.“It is a warning shot,” he said. “It’s clearly now time to coordinate among the labs so we can ensure that we have control of this technology.”Microsoft's approach also reflects an important distinction in the debate. The argument is not necessarily that AI development must stop. It is that increasingly powerful systems should remain subject to human oversight, independent testing and the ability to be corrected or shut down.Anthropic co-founder Jack Clark has gone even further, suggesting that governments may eventually need to require companies to maintain independently verifiable AI “kill switches”.“Should you mandate for companies to definitely have a killswitch? Is that kill switch verifiable by a third party?” he asked.“I think that's the kind of thing society is going to want to know and might want to eventually pass rules around.”One trillion dollars makes slowdown harderThere is another force working against a meaningful slowdown: money.Goldman Sachs Research estimates that global AI-related investment could reach about $1 trillion in 2026. That figure is broader than the frequently cited capital expenditure of US hyperscalers because it includes investment by private companies and businesses outside the US.US hyperscalers alone are expected to spend roughly $800 billion this year, although not all of that spending is directly attributable to AI.This scale of investment creates enormous economic incentives to keep building data centres, buying advanced chips and developing increasingly capable models.The market reaction to Amodei's call showed how deeply AI expectations are embedded in financial markets.Tech-heavy markets fell, while chip stocks came under pressure and some software companies gained.As market analyst Matthew Tuttle put it: “Three rivals now agree that the fastest engine in technology needs a governor. The market still has to ⁠learn how hard that governor will press. A governor is not an emergency brake (but) it stops an engine from running so fast that it tears itself apart.”That may be the most accurate description of the current situation. The industry is not talking about switching AI off. It is talking about putting limits on how quickly the most powerful systems can advance.Is AI waiting for its Hiroshima moment?Now the biggest unresolved question is whether voluntary restraint will be enough. The AI industry is effectively asking governments and companies to design a deterrence and safety framework before a catastrophic event forces them to do it.History offers an uncomfortable comparison. Nuclear weapons did not produce modern arms-control architecture simply because governments understood the theoretical danger. The Hiroshima and Nagasaki bombings, followed by the nuclear arms race, made the consequences tangible and eventually drove efforts towards deterrence, safeguards and international agreements.AI is different, but the policy dilemma has a familiar structure. If the US slows while China accelerates, Washington fears losing a strategic advantage. If China slows while the US accelerates, Beijing faces the same concern. If both refuse to slow, companies have an incentive to race faster because nobody wants to be the player that voluntarily gives up the lead.That is the AI doomerism paradox. Amodei, Altman, Musk and Nadella can agree that frontier AI needs stronger guardrails. Trump can argue that excessive restrictions would hand the advantage to China. Beijing can reject US-led restrictions while simultaneously warning about AI-enabled attacks and espionage.All of them can believe they are acting in the interest of humanity or national security.But if the technology continues advancing faster than governments can build rules around it, the world could eventually be forced to create those rules after a crisis rather than before one.And with roughly $1 trillion in AI investment at stake in 2026, the question is no longer simply whether AI can become dangerous.It is whether the countries and companies building it can agree on how dangerous is too dangerous, before competition makes that decision for them.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: New York City volunteers planted 20,000 marsh seedlings on a dying salt marsh in 2003, but 80% of the site was healthy just two years later
articles.summary: US News: In 2003, a restoration effort at New York City’s Big Egg Marsh took a major step when National Park Service scientists and 100 volunteers planted 20,0.
articles.body: In 2003, a restoration effort at New York City’s Big Egg Marsh took a major step when National Park Service scientists and 100 volunteers planted 20,000 smooth cordgrass seedlings across an area that had been raised with clean sand. The work was part of an experiment to restore a salt marsh in Jamaica Bay, where marshes had been disappearing for decades. The seedlings faced early setbacks, including grazing by geese, tides and marine debris. The vegetation continued to spread. Just two years into the restoration, more than 80% of the experiment site was reported to be vegetated and healthy, offering an encouraging result for the damaged marsh.20,000 seedlings planted on New York City’s dying salt marshOnce the marsh had been raised, the restoration team needed to establish vegetation across the treated area. In October 2003, National Park Service scientists and 100 volunteers planted 20,000 seedlings of smooth cordgrass, known scientifically as Spartina alterniflora. The planting covered the part of Big Egg Marsh where the sand had been sprayed.Smooth cordgrass was particularly suited to the difficult conditions of a salt marsh because it can thrive in high-salinity environments. According to the National Park Service, the plant’s roots trap sediment, allowing it to build up into nutrient-rich peat. That peat creates a stronger foundation for further plant growth, meaning the vegetation could contribute to the longer-term development and stability covering the restored ground.Scientists begin monitoring Big Egg MarshThe planting was followed by systematic monitoring. Scientists established one-metre-by-one-metre plots across Big Egg Marsh and repeatedly returned to record elevation, plant numbers, soil characteristics and the animals present. This allowed researchers to track changes over time rather than judging the restoration from a single observation. Monitoring began in 2004 and continued several times a year through 2008.Geese ate some of the seedlings, while tides washed others away and marine debris such as logs, bottles, plastic bags and straw buried or suffocated some plants. Despite these losses, smooth cordgrass continued to grow, while new seedlings appeared naturally and saltmeadow cordgrass, or salt hay (Spartina patens), also began to establish.80% of the experiment site becomes healthyTwo years into the restoration, the results showed a substantial change across the experiment area. The National Park Service reports that over 80% of its experimental site was vegetated and healthy. This meant that despite the early losses among planted seedlings, vegetation had successfully become established across most of the restoration site.Monitoring continued to provide information about what happened to the marsh over the longer term. In 2021, nearly two decades after restoration began in 2002, Dr George W. Frame returned to Big Egg Marsh to examine its condition. The restoration also helped pave the way for other projects in Jamaica Bay, with efforts across the bay eventually restoring more than 150 acres of marshland.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: I sweated over getting 'A's: Indian-origin founder recounts struggle for 'brown kids' in US, says he cried when he got his first 89
articles.summary: US News: Amid the row over the ethnicity of the students of the University of Texas, Austin, Indian-origin tech founder and an alumnus of the university, Vedan.
articles.body: Amid the row over the ethnicity of the students of the University of Texas, Austin, Indian-origin tech founder and an alumnus of the university, Vedant Nair, shared his experience of growing up in Texas and his struggle as a 'brown kid' to stay a step ahead because of the steep competition. The controversy started after Bo French, a Republican, shared the photo of south Asian students cheering at a football game and asked why so many non-Whites are admitted to the university. Two students, both of Indian origin, spoke out after they found their cheering faces all over the Internet but for racist attacks. It turned out that both of them are US citizens.Nair said Texas law requires 90% of UT's freshman class to be Texas residents. 75% of those in-state seats go to automatic admission on class rank -- and so the question of outsiders getting admission to UT does not even arise.Nair, the co-founder of Miru Robotics, shared how his race started in kindergarten. "Every summer, before the school year started, I had to finish the upcoming year's math textbook.""I sweated over getting As, even in elementary school. One funny memory is walking to my parents' room, crying, to report my first-ever 89 on a report card.""I went to math and science competitions, where I always lost, and came home crying again," he said.Nair clarified that he was not an odd killjoy and he was not even in the top 10% of his class, the competition was that tough."Actually, a lot of the kids worked much harder. I know people who took extra classes (zero period) just to boost their GPA. Who routinely slept 5 hours a night to nail every assignment they had after band practice. Who were distraught when they got a 98 instead of a 100. People who stopped doing things they loved, like sports or arts, because those classes dragged down their GPA," Nair explained.'These are American kids'Nair said the non-White kids in the UT photo are very much American kids who earned their way into the school in the most American way possible. "Kids like this have helped improve UT’s standing on the national stage. They made it out of the pressure cooker and placed well in Finance, Big Tech, and more recently, startups. They meaningfully contribute to the economies of our state and country. You should be proud of them too," he said, adding that the racism could be slightly more intelligent.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Durham councillors who left Reform accused of 'betrayal'
articles.summary: Durham councillors Lyndsey Fox, Nicole Brown and Paul Sexton quit Reform to sit as independents.
articles.body:
Three councillors who have resigned from Reform UK have "conned " voters and "betrayed" those who helped get them elected, the party has said.

Lyndsey Fox, Nicole Brown and Paul Sexton have had their party affiliation changed to independent on the Durham County Council website , although none has given precise reasons for their shift.

It leaves Reform with a small majority, with 51 councillors, on an authority the party emphatically won control of when grabbing 65 seats at last year's election.

Council leader Andrew Husband told the BBC the three former members "have let their residents down" but he offered no explanation for their departures.

Fox, who represents Bishop Auckland, confirmed her departure from Reform to Cathy Newman on Sky News on Tuesday.

The councillor said she had reported a "very serious safeguarding issue" to the party on 14 July but "had heard nothing" since.

Neither she nor Reform has given details on what the safeguarding issue was.

She made further allegations about a "group chat going wild" and said she had been "thinking about resigning for quite a long time".

Sexton, who was elected as an independent in Chester-le-Street before switching to Reform, confirmed he had resigned from the party but declined to say why.

The BBC has also made attempts to contact councillors Brown, who represents Aycliffe South, and Fox but they have yet to respond.

The BBC asked Durham Reform a series of questions including what the safeguarding claims were, what reasons the three had given for resigning and what was being done to address the issue of councillors leaving the party.

In response, Husband said: "These people have let their residents down.

"They have conned them using Reform colours and betrayed the many members who spent their time and money to help get them elected."

articles.title: Carpe diem, Canada: Ottawa’s new global ties can also benefit the US
articles.summary: Canada could become a pivotal economy connecting North America, Europe and Asia.
articles.body:
For decades, Canadian governments have talked about diversifying away from the United States. And for decades, geography has won. Now, Prime Minister Mark Carney appears to be pursuing a much more interesting longer-term strategy. Rather than simply waiting for relations with Washington to improve, Canada is using the disruption to build deeper relationships elsewhere.

The most dramatic example is Europe. Ottawa and Brussels have built a new strategic partnership encompassing energy, critical minerals, technology, digital infrastructure, security and defense, and Canada has become the first non-European participant in the European Union’s SAFE defense initiative.

Yesterday, that effort took a remarkable step forward when European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen told the European Parliament she wanted to open the door for Canada to become the EU’s first “associate member.”

The status does not yet exist and would have to be negotiated and approved by EU member states, but the political signal is unmistakable. This is not just diplomacy. It reflects a growing convergence of interests. Europe wants reliable sources of energy and critical minerals and trusted partners in artificial intelligence, defense and digital infrastructure. It is looking for greater economic security in an increasingly unpredictable world. Canada has much of what Europe needs.

But look west and something equally important is happening. Canada is already part of the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership , giving it preferential access to some of the most important Indo-Pacific economies. It is working to complete a trade agreement with the Association of Southeast Asian Nations and has been deepening bilateral relationships across the region.

For example, earlier this year, Canada and Japan announced a new comprehensive strategic partnership covering energy, critical minerals, defense, semiconductors, batteries, artificial intelligence and other advanced technologies. Japan brings capital, technology and enormous demand for energy and raw materials. Canada brings many of the resources Japan lacks.

The same complementarity exists with South Korea. The two countries are expanding cooperation in liquified natural gas, critical minerals, advanced manufacturing and defense procurement.

Meanwhile, British Columbia is increasingly becoming Canada’s gateway to Asian markets . New energy infrastructure and expanded Pacific port capacity provide Canadian producers with options that simply did not exist a decade ago.

Neither Europe nor Asia can replace the United States, but that notion misses the bigger picture. The strategic question for Canada is not how to substitute one market for another. It is whether Canada can use this moment to position itself at the intersection of three of the most important economic regions on earth.

Canada already occupies an unusual position. It is deeply embedded in the North American economy. It has preferential access to European markets. It is part of the leading trans-Pacific trade agreement. Its coastal positioning and the opening of the Arctic give its geography still greater strategic importance.

Add Canada’s enormous resource base together with clean electricity, sophisticated financial institutions, research universities and growing strengths in artificial intelligence and advanced technologies, and another possibility emerges. Canada could become a pivotal economy connecting North America, Europe and Asia. That does not mean becoming a giant transshipment platform or attempting to play one partner against another. It means becoming a place where the interests of all three increasingly come together.

European capital can help finance Canadian energy, minerals, defense and digital infrastructure. Japanese and Korean investment can help build Canadian critical-mineral, battery and advanced-manufacturing supply chains. Canadian resources can move both east and west. Canadian technology companies can operate across all three markets. And, crucially, Canada remains deeply connected to the U.S.

That last point matters. Indeed, Canada’s relationship with the United States becomes more, not less, valuable if it develops stronger relationships elsewhere. And Canada’s value to its European and Asian partners rises precisely because it remains an integral part of the North American economy.

This is less about reducing trade with America than increasing Canada’s options. Carney has set a goal of doubling Canada’s non-U.S. exports over the coming decade, while his government is pursuing new agreements from Europe to Southeast Asia and India.

There is a political dimension as well. A new U.S. president will take office in January 2029. What that administration’s policy toward Canada will be is impossible to know. But Canada does not need to predict it.

Imagine instead the position Canada could occupy by then. A future Canadian government still integrated into the U.S. economy could approach Washington with a far more substantial strategic relationship with Europe, dramatically stronger links to Asian economies and significantly greater ability to move Canadian energy, resources, technology and capital in multiple directions. That would represent something more important than simply surviving the current trade dispute.

For much of its history, Canada has seen its geography next to an economic superpower as destiny. Perhaps that interpretation has been too narrow. Canada borders the United States. But it also faces Europe across the Atlantic, Asia across the Pacific and an increasingly important Arctic to the north. The opportunity is not to choose among them. It is to connect them.

Duncan Wood is a fellow at the Wilson Center and CEO of Hurst International Consulting.

articles.title: 'Trailblazing' moment as Thickthorn modular bridge takes shape
articles.summary: The "first-of-its-kind" bridge is being pieced together as work continues to improve a key city artery.
articles.body:
The pieces of a "first-of-its-kind" modular bridge are being connected up as work continues to improve a key city artery.

The new bridge is part of a redesign of the A11/A47 Thickthorn junction , near Norwich, with the sections built elsewhere and transported to the site.

This includes six 100-tonne beams measuring 38 metres long, which were built in Ireland and transferred across the Irish Sea to Liverpool, then across the country via road to Norfolk.

National Highways senior project manager Syed Abbas described the build as a "trailblazing" moment for his team, but drivers would face road closures during its installation.

"This is a first-of-its-kind, I'm proud to say, for all of the strategic National Highways network," he added.

The sections of the bridge, connecting Cantley Lane South with Norwich Road in Hethersett, are being connected up with the help of engineering firm Skansa.

A specialist crane, capable of lifting up to 750 tonnes, will begin to move the beams into place on top of the abutments on Friday and road closures will be required from 20:00 BST through to 06:00 on Monday.

Dan Hutchings, project director for Skansa, said: "The construction of the bridge, from start to finish, is about four months, which is significantly quicker than a traditional build on site."

Ongoing maintenance costs are also reduced as it does not have bearings, he said.

Work continues on other aspects of the £200m project, which will also include a new footbridge across the A11, widened slip roads, new link roads, underpasses and more.

Abbas said the scheme was on track to be finished on target by Spring 2028, with the eventual aim of reducing congestion and removing 12,000 vehicles from the Thickthorn roundabout every day.

articles.title: Zelensky appoints new chief prosecutor after predecessor's resignation
articles.summary: Former chief prosecutor Ruslan Kravchenko after searches of his offices by Ukrainian anti-corruption officials.
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has appointed a new acting prosecutor general, after the predecessor resigned over an anti-corruption investigation.

Anton Kovalskyi, 42, was appointed on Thursday to replace Ruslan Kravchenko, who stood down last week following searches of his offices by Ukrainian anti-corruption officials related to illegal call centres in the country.

Officials said they identified a money-laundering scheme led by an official in Kravchenko's office, a claim he rejected.

The investigation into Kravchenko's office is the latest corruption scandal impacting Kyiv during the war against Russia. Accusations have been levelled at several members of Zelensky's inner circle.

According to Ukraine's National Anti-Corruption Bureau (Nabu) and Specialised Anti-Corruption Prosecutor's Office (Sap), the network in Kravchenko's office received money to protect call centres that carried out phone scams and "laundered millions in assets".

The money was then used to buy property, jewellery, and other valuables, according to Nabu.

Kravchenko released a statement denying any involvement and dismissing the allegations as "completely unsubstantiated". He resigned a day later before leaving Ukraine.

He also alleged documents were stolen during the search of his office with the aim of covering up criminal investigations against anti-corruption officials themselves.

Separately, he accused Nabu chief Semen Kryvonos of forging documents in a case nearly 20 years ago.

Both Nabu and Sap denied Kravchenko's claims, while Kryvonos dismissed them as "nonsense" and criticised "fierce" attempts to disrupt corruption probes.

The two anti-corruption agencies claimed it was the latest in an "unprecedented" campaign aimed at disrupting high-profile investigations they were conducting.

Nabu's Kryvonos also claimed that anti-corruption detectives, their offices and vehicles were under surveillance, without giving specific accusations.

He added: "It all looks like an attempt to obstruct the work of Nabu and Sap by gaining access to sensitive information regarding planned investigations."

Nabu and Sap are currently investigating a number of top Ukrainian officials including Zelensky's former chief of staff Andriy Yermak, former ministers and other influential people. Yermak's lawyer has described the allegations against the former official as "baseless".

In 2025, nationwide protests broke out after Zelensky tried to implement reforms that would curb the independence of Nabu and Sap. Zelensky later reinstated their freedom but questions have remained over his commitment to anti-corruption reform.

articles.title: ‘Kosovo’s moves towards Israel are the price of aligning with US policy’
articles.summary: Kosovo’s decision to join a US-led Gaza force exposes the pull of its alliance with Washington, according to analysts.
articles.body:
Kosovo, a small majority-Muslim country in the Balkans, has signed up to United States President Donald Trump’s controversial Board of Peace and the planned International Stabilization Force for Gaza, after Israel gave its approval.

The proposed force is, in theory, expected to help maintain security, support demilitarisation and train Palestinian police, though its mandate and composition remain unclear.

For Kosovo, the decision has a particular resonance.

Its statehood and security depend on international support and NATO protection, as well as the right of a population under pressure from a stronger neighbour to decide its own future. It is now joining a Gaza framework whose legitimacy is contested by Palestinian actors and legal experts, and in which Israel retains decisive influence.

Kosovo was an autonomous province within Serbia in the former Yugoslavia until Slobodan Milosevic stripped it of much of its self-government in 1989. Repression and the political marginalisation of Kosovo Albanians culminated in the 1998-99 war, after the Kosovo Liberation Army launched a rebellion against Serbian and Yugoslav forces.

Serbian and Yugoslav forces responded with killings, expulsions and mass displacement; more than 10,000 Kosovo Albanian civilians were killed. The Hague tribunal later convicted senior Serbian and Yugoslav officials for war crimes and crimes against humanity. After NATO’s 78-day 1999 air campaign, Serbian and Yugoslav forces withdrew.

NATO’s KFOR force, Kosovo’s principal external security guarantor, arrived that June.

Nexhmedin Spahiu, a university professor and political analyst in Pristina, says Kosovo’s approach to Israel reflects a perceived obligation to Washington and, in his view, to the pro-Israel lobby in the US.

NATO and US intervention, Kosovo’s recognition, and the assistance received from the United States are consequences of the lobby’s “influence”, he said. “People in Kosovo feel they have a moral debt … and that is the reason for Kosovo’s approach to Israel.”

For many Kosovo Albanians, the US is associated with the end of repression, the return of refugees and the conditions that made independence possible.

With Serbia still refusing to recognise Kosovo and periodic tensions continuing, US backing and NATO deterrence remain central to Pristina’s security.

“Kosovo’s moves towards Israel are the price of aligning with American policy,” Spahiu said. “It is about repaying old debts.”

Relations with Israel developed within this US-centred logic. Under the Washington agreement of September 2020, Kosovo committed to opening an embassy in Jerusalem. Israel formally recognised Kosovo in February 2021, and Pristina opened its embassy there the following month, becoming the first majority-Muslim country to do so.

Donika Emini, a research fellow at the University of Graz’s Centre for Southeast European Studies, said recognition was “unquestionably a major diplomatic and political achievement” for Kosovo.

Israel’s recognition carried strategic value beyond the bilateral relationship. For Pristina, she added, it helped counter the argument used by states with their own territorial disputes that they could not recognise Kosovo, showing that domestic sovereignty concerns need not prevent such a political decision.

“The relationship has, therefore, been moving beyond recognition towards a broader strategic partnership,” she said, citing Kosovo’s interest in closer security cooperation with Israel.

For Kosovo’s leadership, Israel’s recognition was a concrete victory, while the Jerusalem embassy formed part of a package linked to the first Trump administration. Emini said the calculation was also about strengthening its relationship with Washington.

Artan Muhaxhiri, a Kosovo political analyst, describes this as “proxy politics”: a relationship shaped by, and contingent on, Pristina’s ties with the US rather than an autonomous bilateral policy.

Pristina presents the Gaza role as an opportunity to give back. In March, Prime Minister Albin Kurti said Kosovo was ready to help Gaza because it had benefitted from international forces since 1999.

Emini said Kosovo has long desired to contribute to peace and security, but its lack of UN membership narrows its options.

“Joining a US-led international initiative offers Kosovo something it has been seeking for years: international visibility and an opportunity to demonstrate that it can contribute to international security,” she said. “There is also a degree of reciprocity here.”

She cautioned against a simple comparison with Gaza, where the political and security environment is fundamentally different.

“A significant military role is not a realistic expectation,” he said. Still, participation in high-profile initiatives can help consolidate Kosovo’s state identity, build relationships and advance its wider international integration, he added.

Kosovo’s national story rests on international protection for civilians exposed to state violence and on self-determination.

Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, launched after the Hamas-led attacks of October 7, 2023, has killed tens of thousands of Palestinians. Israel faces a genocide case at the International Court of Justice; the International Criminal Court has issued arrest warrants for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Defence Minister Yoav Gallant over alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity.

For Emini, Pristina has not resolved the tension between its language on Serbia and its position on Gaza.

“The question in Pristina has been less about whether the two positions can be reconciled in purely legal terms, and more about where the United States stands, what Kosovo’s strategic interests are – and what alliances Kosovo can build,” she said.

articles.title: Iran: Account of US Air Force colonel’s rescue ‘fictional’
articles.summary: Iran on Thursday accused the U.S. of fabricating its account of how it rescued an Air Force colonel whose F-15E fighter jet was shot down over Iran in April, calling the claims “fictional and unacceptable.” The service member, referred to by his mission call sign of Bravo, recounted his story of survival earlier this week…
articles.body:
Iran on Thursday accused the U.S. of fabricating its account of how it rescued an Air Force colonel whose F-15E fighter jet was shot down over Iran in April, calling the claims “fictional and unacceptable.”

The service member, referred to by his mission call sign of Bravo, recounted his story of survival earlier this week on CBS’s “60 Minutes.” Bravo told host Norah O’Donnell that he was the weapon-systems officer of the two-man crew when their plane was struck and he plummeted at an estimated 70-100 mph with no parachute as it was damaged by an Iranian shoulder-fired missile.

But Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) spokesperson Brig. Gen. Hossein Mohebbi told Iranian state media that “no sound mind would accept [the U.S.] narrative because it is fictional and unacceptable,” calling it war propaganda.

“The American pilot claimed that he fell at a speed of 160 kilometers per hour and survived, while his parachute did not even open and he crashed into the heart of a mountain,” Mohebbi said, accusing Washington of making up stories about its war achievements in the past.

He added that the U.S. is fabricating the crash and rescue as it is struggling in the more than six-month, deeply unpopular war against Tehran. President Trump has said the conflict will end after the midterm elections.

“The U.S. is embarrassing itself with these actions. These films (pilot interview) will definitely not only fail to bring any achievement … but will also become a source of ridicule,” Mohebbi said.

U.S. Central Command (Centcom) head Adm. Brad Cooper told CBS the crew shot down had been on a mission to conduct a strike on Iranian industrial facilities tied to the country’s drone and missile program.

Bravo said he and his partner, with the mission call sign Alpha, ejected when they could not save the jet. The latter ejected safely, but the colonel landed hard about 5 miles away. Both ended up in Isfahan, Iran, with a U.S. rescue team finding Alpha six hours later.

He added that he was able to alert U.S. forces that he was hurt but still moving and was located by two rescue planes a day later.

The Pentagon earlier received criticism for the highly publicized CBS segment after CNN reported Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and his political appointees in the Pentagon pressured the two airmen to participate.

Three sources told the outlet that the crew members initially were hesitant about doing the interview, with one raising concerns about potentially being ordered to take part. Hegseth then met privately with them and asked whether they wanted to do it willingly rather than being forced, according to CNN.

articles.title: TMC vs TMC: EC bars both factions from using party symbol, name in West Bengal assembly bypolls
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: The Election Commission on Thursday barred both rival Trinamool Congress (TMC) factions from using the party's name and reserved election s.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Election Commission on Thursday barred both rival Trinamool Congress (TMC) factions from using the party's name and reserved election symbol in the upcoming West Bengal Assembly bypolls, according to an interim order.The decision comes ahead of the October 6 bypolls in Nandigram and Rejinagar, where factions led by Mamata Banerjee and Ritabrata Banerjee had fielded candidates while staking claim to the TMC identity and its twin-flowers-on-grass symbol.The poll panel has been hearing competing claims from the two factions over control of the party, its name and election symbol. Both sides have submitted documents and appeared before the Commission during the proceedings.The dispute reached the Election Commission in July after the rival factions staked competing claims to control of the TMC. The Commission subsequently sought responses on issues including organisational control, authorised signatories, party assets, name and election symbol.The issue gained urgency after the EC announced the Nandigram and Rejinagar bypolls for October 6. With nominations closing on September 16, the Commission faced a deadline to determine how the rival factions would contest the elections.The Commission held separate meetings with representatives of both factions on September 12.The Mamata faction was represented by Derek O'Brien, Kalyan Banerjee, Sagarika Ghose, Saket Gokhale and advocate Abhinav Singh. The Ritabrata faction was represented by Ritabrata Banerjee, Akhruzzaman, Arup Roy, Chandrima Bhattacharya and Riju Datt.Both sides maintained that they represented the legitimate TMC and sought recognition of their claim to the party name and symbol.The Mamata faction argued that Banerjee remained the party chairperson and that the national working committee was still within its five-year term.The rival faction contended that the party constitution provided for a three-year term, which it said had ended in February 2025.On September 13, the EC sought final submissions from both factions by 3 pm on September 16, the nomination deadline for the two bypolls. The Commission indicated that another hearing could be held on September 17.At the time, the Mamata faction said that in the absence of an interim order, it would contest using the original TMC symbol. The Ritabrata faction maintained that the EC alone could decide which side was entitled to use the party name and symbol.On September 15, TOI reported that the Commission was likely to issue an interim ruling on September 17.
